title: Chicago, 1893
hook: at the World's Parliament of Religions, Dharmapala and the Zen teacher Soyen Shaku speak

segments.voice: Yesterday: a long poem carried the Buddha's life to English readers. Your line: a dewdrop slipping into the shining sea.
screen: `A DEWDROP SLIPPING INTO THE SHINING SEA.`

segments.voice: A big hall in Chicago, a long row of speakers on the stage. People of many faiths have been invited to stand up, one after another, and explain their own tradition to a crowd of strangers. Some in the seats have read about the Buddha in books like yesterday's poem. Now a Buddhist stands in front of them: a young man from Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, in a plain white robe, Anagarika Dharmapala. Beside him on the program, a Zen abbot from Japan named Soyen Shaku.
screen: `A HALL IN CHICAGO.` → `FAITHS ON ONE STAGE.` → `TWO BUDDHIST VOICES.`

segments.voice: It was called the World's Parliament of Religions, and it met alongside a great fair in Chicago. Its organizers wanted the religions of the world side by side, each in its own words, and they printed the speeches afterward, so we can still read them. Dharmapala had spent his young life working to restore Buddhist places in India, above all Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha woke up under the tree. In Chicago he spoke of the Buddha as a teacher of reason and kindness, whose way was open to anyone willing to practice it. Soyen Shaku was the abbot of a Zen temple in Kamakura, and he did not speak English. His talk, on cause and effect, was put into English and read to the hall for him. Accounts say a young lay student of his helped with the English: D. T. Suzuki, who comes back tomorrow. Why it matters: some in that hall had met the Buddha only in books by outsiders. Here, Buddhists spoke for themselves. The Dhammapada has a line that fits a week of long speeches: "Even though a speech be a thousand (of words), but made up of senseless words, one word of sense is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet." In a hall full of speeches, that was the hope.
screen: `A PARLIAMENT OF RELIGIONS.` · `DHARMAPALA SPEAKS.` · `SOYEN SHAKU, IN ENGLISH.` · `ONE WORD OF SENSE.` · then, large: `THE TEACHING SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Say one true sentence about your own practice, out loud or quietly, maybe: I sit for a couple of minutes most days, or, I'm still working out what my practice is. Say it once, slowly. Then stop, close your eyes, and sit in the quiet after it, the way one word of sense leaves the hearer quiet.
Chicago. Where, at a parliament of faiths, Dharmapala and Soyen Shaku stood up and spoke for the Buddha's teaching in their own voices.
Your line: the teaching speaks. One word of sense outweighs a thousand. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhists in Sri Lanka honor Anagarika Dharmapala as a reviver of the teaching and of the sites in India, and Japanese Zen remembers Soyen Shaku as a teacher who brought Zen before Western listeners.

chat.says: What was special about Buddhists speaking at that big Chicago gathering?
options: Buddhists spoke for themselves, to people who'd known the Buddha from outsiders.
It was the first time anyone in America had heard of the Buddha at all.
Buddhist teachers were asked to debate the other faiths and pick a winner.
chat.meaning: Some listeners had met the Buddha only in books by outsiders. At the Parliament, Dharmapala and Soyen Shaku spoke for the teaching themselves.

Dharmapala.meaning: a Buddhist from Ceylon who worked to restore Bodh Gaya

Soyen Shaku.meaning: a Zen abbot from Kamakura whose talk was read in English

Bodh Gaya.meaning: the place in India where the Buddha woke up under the tree

Kamakura.meaning: a Japanese city where Soyen Shaku's Zen temple stood

Ceylon.meaning: the old name for Sri Lanka
